newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rail industry defends safety record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rail industry defends safety record.

text.p: Despite the high-speed train derailment near New York City this weekend, experts say rail travel remains one of the safest means of transport.

While a number of high-profile accidents involving Amtrak, the U.S. federally-run passenger service, have raised fears of fraying infrastructure and poor maintenance, industry analysts and federal officials say rail safety has actually improved in recent years.
"Amtrak has a quite respectable safety record," said Joseph Sussman, a professor of civil engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

"I wouldn't feel that anyone should change their travel plans for the unsafeness of Amtrak," he added, noting that U.S. rail transport boasts a far lower accident rate compared with trucks and autombiles.

Last Saturday, an Amtrak train bound for New York from Washington, D.C., derailed while crossing a swing bridge, sending two locomotives and four passenger cars plunging down an embankment. No one was killed in the accident, but 32 people were injured.
The National Transportation Safety Board has yet to pinpoint the cause of the accident, but a track malfunction is suspected.

The derailment occurred just a few miles from where two commuter trains collided last February, killing three. Last winter, 11 people were killed when the commuter train they were riding near Washington, D.C., collided head-on with an Amtrak train. In 1993, 47 people were killed in the worst accident in Amtrak's history when a train plunged off a bridge into an Alabama bayou.
But industry groups say these incidents obscure what is largely an outstanding performance record.

"Overall, by far the rail industry has dramatically improved its safety," said John Fitzpatrick, a spokesman for the Association of American Railroads, a Washington, D.C.-based trade group representing Amtrak and private freight carriers.

According to the Federal Railroad Administration, there were four accidents for every million train miles traveled in 1995, down from a rate of 6.3 per million miles in 1985, and just over one-third the number recorded in 1980, the year the U.S. railroad industry was deregulated.
The rate of rail-related passenger deaths and injuries has stayed relatively stable over the past 10 years, but its safety record stacks up well when compared with other means of transport.

In 1994, there were 0.04 deaths per every 100 million rail passenger miles, on par with air travel. By contrast, autombiles registered 0.86 fatalities per every 100 million passenger miles, according to the National Safety Council, an Illinois-based consumer group.
U.S. rail freight traffic, which dwarfs passenger service in terms of miles traveled, has an equally solid safety record, federal regulators say.

"We think the safety record is very strong," said David Bolger, spokesman for the Federal Railroad Administration. "There is a general awareness throughout railroad companies that they can make a lot of money and it can be done efficiently and safely,"
Stephen Klein, who follows the tranport sector for Standard & Poor's Equity Group in New York, notes that railroad companies have stepped up infrastruture spending in the past few years.
"Railroad spending is at fairly high levels (historically)," Klein said. "There is absolutely no reason why they would be scrimping on maintenance."
In 1995, maintenance and equipment expenses represented 45 percent of rail companies' total costs, he said, up from 33 percent 20 years ago.
